## Introduction

This tutorial follows Kyle Walker's [An introduction to tidycensus](https://walker-data.com/census-r/an-introduction-to-tidycensus.html) and [Mapping Census data with R](https://walker-data.com/census-r/mapping-census-data-with-r.html) chapters from [Analyzing US Census Data](https://walker-data.com/census-r/). You will pull data from the American Community Survey through the Census API and turn it into one published page with three graphics: a choropleth map of Texas household income, a ranked chart of state educational attainment, and a scatterplot of California county population and median age.

Use AI however you like throughout. An agentic coding tool works best, since it can read and edit your files directly; a chat-based assistant works too, with more copy/paste.

###

The American Community Survey (ACS) is the Census Bureau's rolling annual survey of about 3.5 million households. Unlike the Decennial Census, which counts everyone every ten years, the ACS estimates characteristics like income, education, and age from a sample — which is why every value arrives with a margin of error.

###

**[tidycensus](https://walker-data.com/tidycensus/)** returns ACS data as a tidy data frame, one row per geography (or per geography-variable). If you also ask for the geographic boundaries, it hands you an **[sf](https://r-spatial.github.io/sf/)** object — a table with a spatial column attached — that **[ggplot2](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/)** can map directly.

### Exercise 3

Every call to `get_acs()` needs a Census API key. Sign up for a free one at the [Census API key signup page](https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html) — the key arrives by email within a few minutes. Click the activation link in that email; the key does not work until you do.

In the R Terminal, run (with your own key in place of `"YOUR-KEY-HERE"`):

```
tidycensus::census_api_key("YOUR-KEY-HERE", install = TRUE)
```

This stores the key in your `.Renviron` file so every future R session finds it automatically. The key is stored on this machine only — on a new machine, install it again with `census_api_key("KEY", install = TRUE, overwrite = TRUE)`.

A running R session does not see the new line until it is restarted. Close the R Terminal (the trash icon on its tab) and open a new one, or run `readRenviron("~/.Renviron")`. Then, in the R Terminal, run:

```
nzchar(Sys.getenv("CENSUS_API_KEY"))
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: introduction-3
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Sign up for a free Census API key at https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html and click the activation link in the email. In the R Terminal, run tidycensus::census_api_key(\"YOUR-KEY-HERE\", install = TRUE) with your own key in place of YOUR-KEY-HERE. Close the R Terminal and open a new one, or run readRenviron(\"~/.Renviron\"). Then, in the R Terminal, run: nzchar(Sys.getenv(\"CENSUS_API_KEY\")) CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```
[1] TRUE
```

###

The key is tied to your email, not a Census account — there is no login to manage. Because `install = TRUE` writes it to `.Renviron` rather than `analysis.qmd`, it never appears in your code or your commits, and every `get_acs()` call in this tutorial picks it up automatically from here on.

## Texas income

Median household income is one of the most-requested ACS variables. Its code is `B19013_001`. In this section you will map it across all 254 Texas counties.

### Exercise 1

Add a chunk to `analysis.qmd` that uses **tidycensus** to get 2020 median household income for every county in Texas, with county geometry attached for mapping, and saves it as `income_tx`. Add `#| message: false` to the chunk to hide the connection messages. Render.

In the R Terminal, run:

```
show_file("analysis.qmd", chunk = "Last")
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Add a chunk to analysis.qmd that uses tidycensus to get 2020 median household income for every county in Texas, with county geometry attached for mapping, and saves it as income_tx. Add #| message: false to the chunk to hide the connection messages. Render. In the R Terminal, run: show_file(\"analysis.qmd\", chunk = \"Last\") CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```
#| message: false
income_tx <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B19013_001",
  state = "TX",
  year = 2020,
  geometry = TRUE
)
```

###

Every ACS request comes down to three choices: the **geographic level** (county here, but census tract, place, or state are equally available), the **variables** — Census table codes like `B19013_001` for median household income — and the **year**, which for the ACS names a 5-year window (2020 means the 2016–2020 estimates, pooled across five years so even small counties have reliable numbers). The first render makes a real network call to the Census API, so it takes a moment.

###

Every county arrives with a `GEOID` (its FIPS code), a `NAME`, the `variable` code, an `estimate`, and a margin of error (`moe`). The `estimate` is the survey's best guess; the `moe` is the half-width of its 90% confidence interval.

### Exercise 6

Start a new working chunk that summarizes median household income and margin of error across the Texas counties. Render.

In the R Terminal, run:

```
show_file("analysis.qmd", chunk = "Last")
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-4
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Start a new working chunk that summarizes median household income and margin of error across the Texas counties. Render. In the R Terminal, run: show_file(\"analysis.qmd\", chunk = \"Last\") CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-4-answer
#| echo: true
income_tx |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarize(
    min_income = min(estimate),
    median_income = median(estimate),
    max_income = max(estimate),
    median_moe = median(moe)
  )
```

###

Every value in the summary is `NA` because one county, Jeff Davis (GEOID 48243), has no 2020 income estimate: the ACS sample there is too small for the Census Bureau to publish a number. `min()`, `median()`, and `max()` return `NA` whenever a missing value is present, and keep doing so until you add `na.rm = TRUE`.

### Exercise 7

Replace the working chunk with the same summary, dropping the missing county before computing each statistic (`na.rm = TRUE`). Render.

In the R Terminal, run:

```
show_file("analysis.qmd", chunk = "Last")
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-12
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Replace the working chunk with the same summary, dropping the missing county before computing each statistic (na.rm = TRUE). Render. In the R Terminal, run: show_file(\"analysis.qmd\", chunk = \"Last\") CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-12-answer
#| echo: true
income_tx |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  summarize(
    min_income = min(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_income = median(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    max_income = max(estimate, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_moe = median(moe, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

###

Across the 253 counties with an estimate, median household income runs from $22,716 in Presidio County to $105,956 in Rockwall County, with a median of $52,683 and a median margin of error of $4,486. That spread is large enough that a map should be interesting, and the next question is whether the high-income counties are scattered randomly or clustered around particular metro areas.

### Exercise 8

Replace the working chunk with a choropleth map of median income across the counties using **ggplot2**. Render and check the map in your Live Server tab.

Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-6
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Replace the working chunk with a choropleth map of median income across the counties using ggplot2. Render and check the map in your Live Server tab. Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-6-answer
#| echo: true
#| message: false
ggplot(income_tx) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = estimate))
```

###

This is a **choropleth** — each county drawn from its boundary and shaded by its income — and the one county left gray, Jeff Davis in far West Texas, is the missing estimate from the summary. Two things make this first version hard to read: the default blue gradient runs dark-to-light in a direction many readers misjudge, and the gray panel with latitude/longitude gridlines adds clutter a map does not need.

### Exercise 9

Improve the map: give it a perceptually uniform color scale (the **[viridis](https://sjmgarnier.github.io/viridis/)** family is the standard choice), a clear title and legend label, a caption naming the data source, and a clean map theme. Render and compare to ours.

Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Improve the map: give it a perceptually uniform color scale (the viridis family is the standard choice), a clear title and legend label, a caption naming the data source, and a clean map theme. Render and compare to ours. Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: texas-income-7-answer
#| echo: true
#| message: false
ggplot(income_tx) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = estimate), color = "white", size = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", name = "Median income") +
  labs(
    title = "Median household income by county, Texas (2020)",
    caption = "Source: ACS 5-year estimates via tidycensus"
  ) +
  theme_void()
```

###

The **viridis** color scales are designed to be perceptually uniform and readable by colorblind viewers, which is why they have become a default for choropleths; **ggplot2** ships them, and the **[RColorBrewer](https://colorbrewer2.org/)** palettes are the other common choice. Reading the finished map, the highest incomes cluster in the suburban counties around the big metros — Austin, Dallas–Fort Worth, and Houston — while many rural counties, especially along the Rio Grande border in the south, carry the lowest median incomes.

A choropleth shades each area by a value, so it is only as honest as the variable behind it. Median household income is a good fit because it is roughly comparable across counties; a raw count like "number of high earners" would mostly track county population and mislead.

## Education by state

Educational attainment lives in ACS table B15003, which breaks the adult population into 24 completed schooling levels from "no schooling" up to "doctorate." In this section you will compare the share of adults with at least a bachelor's degree across all state-level geographies.

### Exercise 1

Add a chunk that uses **tidycensus** to get 2020 educational attainment for state-level geographies and save it as `edu_state`. You need the table total plus the bachelor's-and-higher levels: variables `B15003_001` (total), `B15003_022`, `B15003_023`, `B15003_024`, and `B15003_025`. Pass `summary_var = "B15003_001"` so the total rides along on every row. Add `#| message: false`. Render.

In the R Terminal, run:

```
show_file("analysis.qmd", chunk = "Last")
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: education-by-state-1
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Add a chunk that uses tidycensus to get 2020 educational attainment for state-level geographies and save it as edu_state. You need the table total plus the bachelor's-and-higher levels: variables B15003_001 (total), B15003_022, B15003_023, B15003_024, and B15003_025. Pass summary_var = \"B15003_001\" so the total rides along on every row. Add #| message: false. Render. In the R Terminal, run: show_file(\"analysis.qmd\", chunk = \"Last\") CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```
#| message: false
edu_state <- get_acs(
  geography = "state",
  variables = c("B15003_001", "B15003_022", "B15003_023", "B15003_024", "B15003_025"),
  year = 2020,
  geometry = FALSE,
  summary_var = "B15003_001"
)
```

###

These five variable codes report *completed* degrees, not enrollment. `B15003_022` through `B15003_025` are bachelor's, master's, professional, and doctorate degrees — four separate, non-overlapping levels — so adding them counts everyone with at least a bachelor's.

### Exercise 3

Replace the working chunk with code that collapses `edu_state` to one row per geography. Compute the percentage of adults with at least a bachelor's degree, then print the table sorted from highest to lowest percentage. Render.

In the R Terminal, run:

```
show_file("analysis.qmd", chunk = "Last")
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: education-by-state-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Replace the working chunk with code that collapses edu_state to one row per geography. Compute the percentage of adults with at least a bachelor's degree, then print the table sorted from highest to lowest percentage. Render. In the R Terminal, run: show_file(\"analysis.qmd\", chunk = \"Last\") CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: education-by-state-8-answer
#| echo: true
edu_state |>
  group_by(GEOID, NAME) |>
  summarize(
    percent = 100 * sum(estimate[variable != "B15003_001"]) / unique(summary_est),
    adults = unique(summary_est),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(desc(percent))
```

###

The District of Columbia sits far above the states, at about 60%, because it is a city-like jurisdiction with a highly educated labor market; the lowest geography is about 21% and the middle one around 31%. Raw counts would have put California first simply because it has so many adults, which is why the share, not the count, is the measure to compare.

### Exercise 5

Improve the chart: add a clear title, axis label, source caption, percent-formatted axis labels, and a cleaner theme. Render and compare to ours.

Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: education-by-state-12
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Improve the chart: add a clear title, axis label, source caption, percent-formatted axis labels, and a cleaner theme. Render and compare to ours. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: education-by-state-12-answer
#| echo: true
edu_state |>
  group_by(GEOID, NAME) |>
  summarize(
    percent = 100 * sum(estimate[variable != "B15003_001"]) / unique(summary_est),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, percent), y = percent, fill = percent)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Adults with a bachelor's degree or higher by state-level geography (2020)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Share of adults 25 and over",
    caption = "Source: ACS 5-year estimates via tidycensus"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

###

The finished chart shows a regional and institutional pattern that a table makes hard to scan: the highest values cluster in the District of Columbia and several Northeastern or knowledge-economy states, while the lowest values are concentrated in parts of Appalachia and the South. Because this is a percentage of adults 25 and over, the comparison is not just a population-size ranking.

This section used the same table as a county-level education map would use, but changed the geography to states and territories. That is one of **tidycensus**'s central ideas: the variables define what you measure, and the geography defines the units you compare.

## California median age

Not every Census question is a map. Here you will pull median age and total population for California counties, then ask whether larger counties tend to be younger or older. This section also revisits the reshaping step that long-format ACS data often needs.

### Exercise 1

Add a chunk that uses **tidycensus** to get 2020 median age and total population for every county in California, naming the variables `median_age` (`B01002_001`) and `population` (`B01003_001`). ```

```
  variables = c(median_age = "B01002_001", population = "B01003_001"),
  state = "CA",
```

You can give each variable a readable name — `median_age`, `population` — instead of carrying raw codes like `B01002_001` around, which makes everything downstream easier to read. And because this section does not draw boundaries, skipping the geometry download is the right call — there is no reason to pull polygons you will not use.

### Exercise 3

Replace the working chunk with code that reshapes `age_ca` to one row per county, with one column for `median_age` and one for `population`. Print the table sorted from largest to smallest population. Render.

In the R Terminal, run:

```
show_file("analysis.qmd", chunk = "Last")
```

CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: california-median-age-5
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Replace the working chunk with code that reshapes age_ca to one row per county, with one column for median_age and one for population. Print the table sorted from largest to smallest population. Render. In the R Terminal, run: show_file(\"analysis.qmd\", chunk = \"Last\") CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: california-median-age-5-answer
#| echo: true
age_ca |>
  select(NAME, variable, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = estimate) |>
  arrange(desc(population))
```

###

**Reshaping** turns repeated variable/value rows into one column per variable, so each of the 58 counties now has `median_age` and `population` side by side. Population runs from tiny Alpine County to Los Angeles County, while median age varies by only a few decades.

### Exercise 4

Replace the working chunk with a scatterplot of county population against median age. Render and look at the relationship.

Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: california-median-age-7
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Replace the working chunk with a scatterplot of county population against median age. Render and look at the relationship. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: california-median-age-7-answer
#| echo: true
#| message: false
age_ca |>
  select(NAME, variable, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = estimate) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = population, y = median_age)) +
  geom_point()
```

###

The rough scatterplot has the right variables — most counties sit in the mid-30s to mid-40s, with a few much older ones — but the population axis is hard to read because Los Angeles County is so much larger than most counties. A log scale is a better fit when one variable spans several orders of magnitude.

### Exercise 5

Improve the scatterplot: use a log-scaled population axis, label the largest counties, add a title, clean axis labels, and a source caption. Render and compare to ours.

Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: california-median-age-8
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Improve the scatterplot: use a log-scaled population axis, label the largest counties, add a title, clean axis labels, and a source caption. Render and compare to ours. Take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: california-median-age-8-answer
#| echo: true
#| message: false
age_ca |>
  select(NAME, variable, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = estimate) |>
  mutate(label = if_else(min_rank(desc(population)) <= 8, NAME, "")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = population, y = median_age)) +
  geom_point(color = "#2c7fb8", alpha = 0.75, size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.05, check_overlap = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_x_log10(
    labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale()),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.25))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Smaller California counties tend to be older (2020)",
    x = "Population (log scale)",
    y = "Median age",
    caption = "Source: ACS 5-year estimates via tidycensus"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

###

The final plot shows a negative relationship: California's largest counties are mostly in the 30s, while many of the oldest counties are small. The log scale keeps Los Angeles County visible without flattening every smaller county into the left edge of the chart.

Median age is itself an ACS estimate with a margin of error, just like income. For large counties the margin is tiny, but for the smallest counties a difference of a year or two between counties may be inside the margin and not real.

## Summary

This tutorial followed the **tidycensus** chapters of [Analyzing US Census Data](https://walker-data.com/census-r/) by Kyle Walker. You pulled American Community Survey data through the Census API with **tidycensus**, learned how ACS estimates carry margins of error, reshaped long-format results into the wide shape that plotting needs, and built one published page with three graphics: a choropleth map of Texas household income, a ranked chart of state educational attainment, and a scatterplot of California county population and median age.

````{verbatim}
```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
```

```{r}
#| message: false
#| cache: true
income_tx <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = "B19013_001",
  state = "TX",
  year = 2020,
  geometry = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
#| message: false
ggplot(income_tx) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = estimate), color = "white", size = 0.1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", name = "Median income") +
  labs(
    title = "Median household income by county, Texas (2020)",
    caption = "Source: ACS 5-year estimates via tidycensus"
  ) +
  theme_void()
```

```{r}
#| message: false
edu_state <- get_acs(
  geography = "state",
  variables = c("B15003_001", "B15003_022", "B15003_023", "B15003_024", "B15003_025"),
  year = 2020,
  geometry = FALSE,
  summary_var = "B15003_001"
)
```

```{r}
edu_state |>
  group_by(GEOID, NAME) |>
  summarize(
    percent = 100 * sum(estimate[variable != "B15003_001"]) / unique(summary_est),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, percent), y = percent, fill = percent)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(scale = 1)) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "plasma", guide = "none") +
  labs(
    title = "Adults with a bachelor's degree or higher by state-level geography (2020)",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Share of adults 25 and over",
    caption = "Source: ACS 5-year estimates via tidycensus"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```

```{r}
#| message: false
age_ca <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(median_age = "B01002_001", population = "B01003_001"),
  state = "CA",
  year = 2020,
  geometry = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
age_ca |>
  select(NAME, variable, estimate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = variable, values_from = estimate) |>
  mutate(label = if_else(min_rank(desc(population)) <= 8, NAME, "")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = population, y = median_age)) +
  geom_point(color = "#2c7fb8", alpha = 0.75, size = 2.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), hjust = -0.05, check_overlap = TRUE, size = 3) +
  scale_x_log10(
    labels = scales::label_number(scale_cut = scales::cut_short_scale()),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.25))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Smaller California counties tend to be older (2020)",
    x = "Population (log scale)",
    y = "Median age",
    caption = "Source: ACS 5-year estimates via tidycensus"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()
```
````

###

**tidycensus** accepts a state as a name (`"Texas"`), a postal code (`"TX"`), or a FIPS code (`"48"`), and will aggregate to whatever geographic level you ask for — county here, but also census tract, place, or state. The same request scales from a single county map to a national tract-level analysis without changing the approach.
